claim: A learned predictor trained on historical multi-agent workflow traces plus the current request's context can forecast the next agent invocation with 0.94 accuracy at a 1-step horizon and 0.77 accuracy at a 3-step horizon.
stance_target: probabilistic sequence prediction from agent-trace history is achievable with high accuracy at short horizons and degrades at longer horizons
scope_conditions: HoVer dataset with LangChain framework; trained on 1,000 traces, tested on 500
quoted_support: On the HoVer dataset with the LangChain framework, training on 1K traces achieves an accuracy of 0.94 at 1-step and 0.77 at 3-step (500-trace test set).

claim: Static, predefined agent-invocation DAGs (the approach used by SOTA baseline KVFlow) fail on realistic dynamic multi-agent workflows because the actual sequence of invoked agents is runtime-dependent (e.g., a Tester sending code back for rewriting, a Retriever spawning new sub-queries), motivating probabilistic prediction instead of static assumption.
stance_target: static workflow-graph assumptions are sufficient for managing or predicting agent skill/tool sequences
quoted_support: This design rests on a strong assumption: the future invocation order of agents is known a priori. This assumption fails on realistic dynamic workloads, where workflows are runtime-dependent. For example, a Tester may send the code back for rewriting; and a Retriever may spawn new sub-queries based on intermediate results.

claim: Fusing cross-workflow historical transition patterns with per-request semantic context, plus predicting multiple steps ahead rather than one step, is necessary to avoid myopic predictions that cannot distinguish cache that will be reused later (e.g. via a retry loop) from cache that is truly useless.
stance_target: design principle: combine population-level trace statistics with per-instance context, and predict multiple steps ahead, for effective probabilistic skill-sequence prediction
quoted_support: Multi-step horizon, which is motivated by the fact that cache reuse distances in agentic workflows can span several invocations (e.g., across a retry loop), so a single-step predictor cannot distinguish cache that will be reused later from useless cache.

claim: Because agentic workloads are inherently hard to predict due to LLM stochastic decoding propagating uncertainty along the workflow path, a prediction-consuming system must act conservatively: PBKV's conservative prefetching (consuming only idle GPU memory/bandwidth) is safer than aggressive prefetching, which degrades below the conservative baseline as prediction noise or prefetch budget grows.
stance_target: autonomous probabilistic prediction systems must bound downside risk via conservative resource use rather than trusting predictions fully
scope_conditions: HoVer+LangChain workload, Qwen3-32B, concurrency 72, controlled noise-injection ablation
quoted_support: aggressive prefetching only achieves a marginal and unstable advantage over conservative prefetching when the prediction accuracy is sufficiently high (i.e., the noise level is below 20%). However, dynamic multi-agent workflows are inherently hard to predict... Therefore, PBKV adopts conservative prefetching to obtain stable gains.

claim: A prediction-driven cache/resource management system (PBKV) built on probabilistic next-agent forecasting achieves up to 1.85x speedup over LRU on dynamic multi-agent workflows and up to 1.26x speedup over the static-DAG-based SOTA baseline KVFlow.
stance_target: probabilistic prediction of agent/skill sequences from trace history yields measurable production-relevant performance gains over both naive and static-assumption baselines
quoted_support: Experiments on three workflow benchmarks show that PBKV achieves up to 1.85x speedup over LRU on dynamic workflows, and up to 1.26x speedup over the SOTA baseline KVFlow on the static workflow.

claim: Under sustained load on the HoVer+LangChain workload with Qwen3-14B at concurrency 72, LRU's cache hit rate collapses to below 30% (around 10% in the steady-state interior), while PBKV's lifecycle-aware eviction alone reaches 66.01% hit rate and the full PBKV system (adding speculative prefetching) reaches 69.10%.
stance_target: prediction-informed cache management substantially outperforms recency-based heuristics under realistic agentic load
scope_conditions: HoVer + LangChain workload, Qwen3-14B, concurrency limit 72
quoted_support: achieves a hit rate below 30% on both models... pushing the hit rate to 66.01%... attains a hit rate of 69.10%.

claim: Across predictor architectures tested (MLP, GCN, Markov, kNN, linear baselines, and a learned transformer-based model), prediction accuracy monotonically determines downstream cache-hit-rate gains, and the learned predictor outperforms every baseline family at every lookahead horizon while continuing to improve with more training data, whereas the parameter-free Markov baseline saturates early.
stance_target: learned sequence predictors over agent-trace history scale better than simple Markov-chain baselines for skill/agent-sequence prediction
scope_conditions: ablation across predictor backbones and training-set sizes
quoted_support: Our predictor leads every baseline at every [horizon]... learning-based [predictors] scale with data while the Markov baseline saturates within [limited data].
